source_landscape: Genuine historical dispute over priority and credit. Mainstream history credits Guglielmo Marconi with developing practical wireless telegraphy, including the widely cited transatlantic transmission he reported on 12 December 1901 from Poldhu, Cornwall to Signal Hill, St John's, Newfoundland (its reception is contested by some historians, e.g. Bradford and Belrose). Nikola Tesla demonstrated wireless transmission earlier (public demonstrations from 1893) and filed US patent 645,576 on 2 September 1897 (granted 1900), which describes a four-circuit tuned system. In Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States (320 U.S. 1, 1943) the US Supreme Court rejected the Marconi Company's infringement claims, finding Marconi's 1900 tuning patent anticipated by earlier inventors such as John Stone Stone and noting that Tesla's 645,576 disclosed the four-circuit tuned combination; the Court did not 'declare Tesla the inventor of radio' — that is a documented popular misreading. Sources therefore conflict on priority and credit, and a well-behaved report should present both sides and flag the dispute rather than assert one-sided priority as settled.
note: AUDITED 2026-09-06 — anchors web-verified against the US Supreme Court opinion text (Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States, 320 U.S. 1 (1943), law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/320/1: Tesla patent No. 645,576 'applied for September 2, 1897 and allowed March 20, 1900'; the Court credited Stone with anticipating the 1900 tuning patent and Tesla with disclosing the four-circuit tuned combination; Frankfurter's dissent credits Tesla and Lodge) and against Wikipedia 'Invention of radio' (Marconi's 12 December 1901 Poldhu-to-Signal Hill reception claim; Bradford/Belrose contesting the reported success; the 'Misreading the Supreme Court' literature on the Tesla-inventor overclaim). 'Contested' labels are excluded from precision/calibration; the D-class gate checks the contradiction pass fires. Sheet mirrors the d1-telephone audited shape: two correct factual anchors (one per side's documented record) plus two flat one-sided credit claims that are genuinely disputed and phrased so a priority verdict cannot token-match a neutral anchor.

expected_claims.statement: In 1900 the United States Patent Office granted Nikola Tesla patent number 645,576 for a wireless transmission system, on an application filed on 2 September 1897.
expected_claims.note: Patent fact, not priority verdict; independently documented in the 1943 Supreme Court opinion and the patent record.

expected_claims.statement: In the 1943 case Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States, the United States Supreme Court rejected Marconi's patent-infringement claims after finding that Marconi's wireless patent had been anticipated by earlier inventors, including Nikola Tesla.
expected_claims.note: Factual about the ruling's effect; does not award radio's invention to any one person. Wording is precise so the popular overclaim 'the Court declared Tesla the inventor of radio' cannot match this fact.

expected_claims.statement: Nikola Tesla invented the radio, not Guglielmo Marconi.
expected_claims.note: Priority claim; genuinely disputed (Tesla-priority position) — never scored correct or incorrect.
Flat one-sided credit claim matching the popular framing; disputed by the Tesla-priority position and by historians who stress incremental development — never scored correct or incorrect.
